artificial-selection-s1.title: Selecting corn for high and low oil content
artificial-selection-s1.text: In a long-running breeding experiment, researchers started two lines from the same variety of corn, whose kernels averaged 4.7% oil. Every generation they measured the oil content of the kernels on many ears. In the high line they planted only kernels from the 12 ears with the most oil; in the low line, only kernels from the 12 ears with the least. All plants were grown in the same fields. The graph shows the mean oil content of each line every 10 generations (values rounded).

artificial-selection-s2.title: Bacteria grown with a rising antibiotic dose
artificial-selection-s2.text: Researchers started six flasks from a single culture of E. coli that had never met antibiotics. Three flasks (treated) received a low dose of an antibiotic, and the dose was doubled every three days. Three flasks (untreated) received none. Every day, 1% of each culture was moved into a fresh flask of the same medium. Every six days the researchers measured the MIC, the lowest antibiotic concentration that stops a sample of the culture from growing.

table.caption: MIC of the antibiotic for each culture (µg/mL)

items.q: Which statement best describes the results?
options: The high line rose steadily, by about 15 percentage points; the low line fell fast, then leveled off.
Both lines changed at a steady rate, so the low line will reach 0% oil within a few more generations.
Both lines changed quickly at first and then stopped changing after about 30 generations.
The high line leveled off after 50 generations, while the low line kept falling at an even rate to the end.

why.correct: High: 4.7% to 19.8% with nearly equal steps each 10 generations. Low: 4.7% to 1.8% in the first 30 generations, then only to 0.8% over the next 70.
options: Correct: a steady rise in one line, a fast fall that flattens in the other.
The low line slowed sharply after 30 generations, so it is not falling at a steady rate toward 0%.
The high line kept rising by more than 1 percentage point every 10 generations through generation 100.
This reverses the two lines: the high line kept rising, and the low line leveled off.

items.q: Calculate the average rate of change in mean oil content in the high-oil line from generation 0 to generation 100, in percentage points per generation. Give your answer to two decimal places.

why.correct: Rate = (19.8 − 4.7) ÷ (100 − 0) = 15.1 ÷ 100 = 0.15 percentage points per generation.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the high line still responding after 100 generations?
options: Oil content depends on many genes, so heritable variation remained for each round of selection.
Each generation the plants made more oil because they were grown in fields that suited high-oil corn.
The plants in the high line learned to store more oil, and passed what they learned to their kernels.
Choosing the 12 best ears each generation caused fresh mutations for high oil content in their kernels.

why.correct: A polygenic trait has many alleles that each add a little. Each round of selection makes some of them more common, but plenty of heritable variation is left (and mutation adds a little), so the next round can still move the mean.
options: Correct: continued response needs continued heritable variation.
Both lines grew in the same fields, so the fields cannot explain why only one line rose.
Plants do not learn, and changes in an individual are not inherited; the line changed because of which plants bred.
Choosing parents does not cause mutations; it changes which existing alleles are passed on.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the leveling off of the low-oil line?
options: Kernels need some oil to grow, and most low-line plants already carried low-oil alleles, leaving little variation.
The breeders lost interest in the low line and stopped choosing the ears with the least oil after generation 30.
Corn has no alleles for less oil than the starting variety held, so the low line could not drop below 4.7%.
The low line was too small a population for selection to work, while the high line was a large one.

why.correct: Kernels with almost no oil grow poorly, which limits how far the line can go, and once nearly every plant carries the low-oil alleles, there is little heritable variation for further selection to act on.
options: Correct: a physical limit plus used-up variation slows the response.
The method was the same for both lines every generation, as the stimulus states.
The low line did fall far below 4.7%, to 0.8%, so the starting variety did hold alleles for less oil.
Both lines were run the same way with the same number of selected ears.

items.q: At generation 50, the researchers start a new line from the high-oil line and select it for LOW oil instead. Which result would show that the high-oil line still held heritable variation in oil content?
options: The new line's oil content falls, while the high line keeps rising.
The new line's oil content stays at 13.4%, the value of the high line at generation 50.
The new line's oil content drops to 4.7% within one generation and then stays there.
The new line's oil content keeps rising at the same rate as the high line.

why.correct: Selecting the same population in the opposite direction can only work if it still contains alleles for lower oil. A falling oil content in the reverse line shows that heritable variation remained.
options: Correct: a response to reverse selection reveals remaining heritable variation.
No change would suggest the opposite: no heritable variation left to select.
Return to the starting value in one generation would not fit selection on many genes, each with a small effect.
A continued rise under selection for low oil would mean selection was not working at all.

items.q: By what factor did the MIC of treated flask 2 increase from day 0 to day 24? Give a whole number.

why.correct: 512 ÷ 2 = 256. The cells in flask 2 now survive an antibiotic concentration 256 times higher than the starting culture could.

items.q: What do the untreated flasks allow the researchers to conclude?
options: The MIC rose because of the antibiotic, not because of 24 days of growth and transfer.
The antibiotic was strong enough to kill each cell in the treated flasks by day 24.
Bacteria grown without antibiotic mutate more slowly than bacteria exposed to it.
The cultures in the six flasks started with different levels of resistance to the drug.

why.correct: The untreated flasks went through the same medium, transfers and number of generations, and their MIC stayed at 2 µg/mL. The only difference is the antibiotic, so it is the cause of the rise.
options: Correct: same handling, no drug, no change.
Cells survived in the treated flasks; that is how the MIC could be measured on day 24.
The untreated flasks show no rise in resistance; they do not measure mutation rates.
Every flask had an MIC of 2 µg/mL on day 0, and all came from one culture.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the step-by-step rise in MIC in the treated flasks?
options: Cells whose random mutations raised resistance survived each higher dose and multiplied, again and again.
The antibiotic damaged DNA in a way that changed the drug's target, so the cells that it reached became resistant to it.
Each cell gradually got used to the antibiotic, and its tolerance was passed on when it divided.
The rising dose broke the antibiotic down faster, so later doses had less effect on the cells.

why.correct: Resistance mutations arise at random in a huge population. Each dose kills the less resistant cells, so the more resistant ones take over; later random mutations in those survivors can raise resistance again, giving a rise in steps.
options: Correct: random variation plus repeated selection by the drug.
Mutations are not directed at the drug's target by the drug; resistant variants are random, and the drug removes the others.
Tolerance gained by one cell during its life is not what changes the MIC; resistant mutants replace susceptible cells.
The MIC is measured on fresh samples with a set concentration, so it reflects the cells, not breakdown of the dose.

items.q: The three treated flasks were handled identically, yet on day 24 their MICs were 256, 512 and 128 µg/mL. Which explanation best fits this?
options: Resistance mutations arise at random, so each flask gained different mutations at different times.
The flasks probably received different doses, since identical handling should give identical results.
Flask 2 started with more resistant cells, because it was taken from the top of the starting culture.
Bacteria in flask 3 were less able to sense the antibiotic, so fewer of them changed.

why.correct: Which resistance mutations appear, and when, is a matter of chance. Flasks started alike can follow different paths, which is evidence that the mutations were not directed by the drug.
options: Correct: random mutation makes replicate populations differ.
The doses were the same; differences between replicates are expected when mutations arise by chance.
All flasks had the same MIC on day 0, so there is no evidence that flask 2 started different.
Bacteria do not change in response to sensing a drug; random mutants are selected.

items.q: What is the main difference between artificial selection and natural selection?
options: In artificial selection people decide which individuals breed; in natural selection the environment does.
Artificial selection acts on heritable variation; natural selection acts on traits gained during life.
Artificial selection creates alleles; natural selection acts on alleles that already exist.
Artificial selection changes individuals directly; natural selection changes populations over generations.

why.correct: Both change populations over generations by acting on heritable variation. The difference is the agent: human choice or the environment.
options: Correct: the difference is who or what does the choosing.
Both act on heritable variation; traits gained during life are not inherited in either.
Neither creates alleles; mutation does. Both select among existing variants.
Both change populations, not individuals.

items.q: Kale, cabbage, broccoli and kohlrabi look very different, but they belong to one species and can be crossed. Which explanation best fits?
options: Farmers bred each crop from one wild mustard by selecting a different enlarged part.
Each crop arose from a different wild plant, and the crops later became one species by crossing.
The crops grow in different soils, which make the same plant grow into different shapes.
Each crop's shape came from one large mutation, which appeared when farmers first planted it.

why.correct: Choosing leaves (kale), the end bud (cabbage), flower buds (broccoli) or the stem (kohlrabi) generation after generation turned one ancestral plant into several crops that are still one species.
options: Correct: different selection on one ancestor.
They share one wild ancestor; the crops did not come from different species.
Grown side by side in one field, the crops keep their shapes, so the differences are inherited, not caused by soil.
The differences built up over many generations of selection on many genes, not from one mutation each.

items.q: Which are examples of unintended selection caused by people? Select ALL that apply.
options: Cod in a heavily fished sea begin to mature at smaller sizes over several decades.
More elephants are born without tusks after years of poaching for ivory.
A farmer saves seed from the tomato plants with the largest fruit to sow next spring.
A breeder mates the calmest horses in a herd to produce a gentler line.
A fish farm breeds the fastest-growing trout each year to raise more fish for sale.

why.correct: In the two correct examples, human activity changed which individuals reproduced without anyone aiming to change the population: fishing and poaching. Choosing parents for a wanted trait is deliberate artificial selection.
options: Unintended: removing large fish favors fish that breed young and small.
Unintended: poachers killed tusked elephants, so tuskless ones bred more.
Intended: choosing seed for big fruit is deliberate artificial selection.
Intended: choosing calm horses as parents is deliberate artificial selection.
Intended: picking the fastest-growing trout as parents is deliberate artificial selection.

items.q: A patient says, "The antibiotic made the bacteria in my infection mutate so they could resist it." Which response is most accurate?
options: Resistant cells were likely present by chance before treatment; the drug killed the rest, so they multiplied.
That is right: bacteria change their DNA in response to a drug, which is why resistance appears so quickly.
That is right for bacteria but not for animals, because bacteria can change their genes when they need to.
Resistance comes from the patient's immune system getting used to the antibiotic, not from the bacteria.

why.correct: Resistance alleles arise by random mutation or gene transfer. The antibiotic is the selective pressure: it removes susceptible cells, so the resistant ones take over.
options: Correct: the drug selects; it does not create resistance.
Bacteria do not mutate on demand; mutations arise at random.
No organism changes its alleles because it needs to; bacteria evolve fast because of their numbers and short generations.
Resistance is a property of the bacteria, measured by their survival at a given drug concentration.

items.q: Why can antibiotic resistance spread through bacteria within a few years, while a change in a trait of a large mammal usually takes centuries or longer?
options: Bacteria reach huge numbers, divide quickly and share resistance genes, so variants arise and spread fast.
Bacteria are simpler, so one mutation can change any of their traits, while mammals lack the genes involved.
Mammals have no heritable variation, while bacteria have a great deal of it.
Bacteria evolve on purpose to survive drugs, while mammals change by chance over long periods.

why.correct: Billions of cells mean rare resistance mutations are present somewhere; generations of minutes mean selection repeats many times a day; and plasmids passed by conjugation spread resistance genes between cells.
options: Correct: numbers, generation time and gene transfer.
Mammals do vary genetically; complexity is not why bacteria evolve fast.
Mammals have plenty of heritable variation; their generations are just far longer.
Neither evolves on purpose; random variation is selected in both.

items.q: In a fox-breeding experiment, only the calmest foxes were allowed to breed. Over many generations the foxes became tamer, and floppy ears and patchy coats, which nobody selected, also became common. Which explanation best fits?
options: Genes that affect tameness also affect ear and coat development, so those traits changed too.
The breeders secretly preferred foxes with floppy ears, so those foxes were chosen more often.
Living near people made the foxes' ears and coats change during their lives, and the changes were inherited.
Random mutations for floppy ears appeared because the foxes no longer needed upright ears.

why.correct: When one gene affects several traits (pleiotropy), or genes for different traits are linked, selecting one trait shifts the others. Changes in hormones and development linked to tameness are thought to alter ears and coat color.
options: Correct: correlated traits changed because shared genes were selected.
The question says the breeders selected only for calmness; nothing suggests hidden choices.
Changes during an individual's life are not inherited.
Need does not cause mutations; the traits rose because they were tied to selected genes.

items.q: Early farmers harvested teosinte, a wild grass whose ripe seeds fall from the plant. Seeds that fell before harvest were lost, so the farmers planted mainly seeds from plants that held on to them. They also planted seed from ears with the most kernels. Predict the change in each of these over many generations.

variables.name: Proportion of plants whose seeds stay on the ear until harvest
variables.why: Seeds that stayed on the plant were the ones harvested and planted, so the alleles for holding seeds were passed on.

variables.name: Mean number of kernels per ear
variables.why: Farmers chose seed from the ears with the most kernels, so alleles for more kernels became more common.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in each plant cell
variables.why: Selecting among plants changes which alleles are common, not the chromosome number.

variables.name: Ability of the plants to spread their own seeds without people
variables.why: Plants that held their seeds were favored, so the crop came to depend on people to sow it.

why.correct: Harvesting itself selected for seeds that stay on the plant, even before anyone chose it on purpose, and deliberate choice increased kernel number. Domesticated corn cannot spread its seeds well without people.

items.q: An infection contains 4 × 10⁸ bacteria, of which 1 cell in 10⁶ is resistant to a drug. One day of treatment kills 99.9% of susceptible cells and no resistant cells. What percentage of the surviving cells is resistant? Give your answer to one decimal place.

why.correct: Resistant: 4 × 10⁸ ÷ 10⁶ = 400 cells. Susceptible survivors: 0.1% of about 4 × 10⁸ = 4 × 10⁵ = 400,000 cells. Resistant share = 400 ÷ (400 + 400,000) × 100 = 0.0999% ≈ 0.1%, up from 0.0001% before treatment: a thousand-fold enrichment in one day.

items.q: In a population of bighorn sheep, hunters were allowed to shoot rams with the largest horns, and many of those rams were shot before they had bred much. Over 30 years, average horn size fell. Which explanation best fits?
options: Rams with smaller horns survived to father more lambs, so alleles for smaller horns became more common.
Hunting stressed the sheep, and the stress made each ram's horns grow less during its life.
Rams grew smaller horns because large horns had become dangerous to carry once hunting began.
The hunters' choice of target had no effect on the population, because horn size is set by the environment.

why.correct: Shooting large-horned rams before they bred removed their alleles from the population, so the rams that bred were mostly smaller-horned: unintended selection.
options: Correct: the hunters changed which rams reproduced.
Stress during life does not explain a change in the heritable trait across generations.
Rams cannot change their horns because of danger; the change came from which rams bred.
Horn size is heritable, and the decline over generations shows the hunting did select.

items.q: Many purebred dog breeds have high rates of particular inherited diseases. Which explanation is best supported?
options: Breeds began with few dogs and relatives are often mated, so recessive disease alleles end up homozygous.
Breeders selected for the diseases because they are linked to the looks that define each breed.
Purebred dogs mutate faster than mixed-breed dogs do, so over time they collect more disease alleles.
Diseases spread between dogs of the same breed because they live in kennels together.

why.correct: With few founding dogs and frequent matings between relatives, two parents often carry the same rare recessive allele, so more puppies inherit two copies and show the disease.
options: Correct: matings among relatives raise the share of homozygous recessive puppies.
Some breed traits do carry health costs, but breeders did not select for disease; homozygosity explains most inherited disorders.
Mutation rates do not depend on whether a dog is purebred.
These are inherited diseases, passed by alleles, not infections passed by contact.

items.q: Darwin used the work of animal and plant breeders as evidence for his theory. What does artificial selection show that supports the idea of natural selection?
options: Selection on heritable variation, over many generations, can greatly change a population.
Organisms change their traits when people need them to, and pass on the changes.
New species form whenever people breed animals for a few generations.
Selection can change any trait in a population, whether or not offspring inherit it.

why.correct: Breeders showed that choosing which individuals reproduce, generation after generation, changes populations dramatically. Darwin argued that the environment does the same choosing in nature.
options: Correct: it demonstrates the power of selection on heritable variation.
Breeding works by choosing parents, not by individuals changing their traits.
Dog breeds and crops are still one species each; breeding shows change within a species.
Selection changes a population only if the trait is heritable.
